submission.natural_language_explanation: The positive pole is a retrospective lexical detector: it fires when the current token is one of a learned set of common English predicate words, above all everyday verb word-forms of the take/get/give/keep/help/make/find/save/protect/provide/create/turn/go/come/run/look/try/think family (and every inflection of them: take/takes/taking/took/taken, become/became/becomes, help/helps/helped, find/finds/found), plus a few degree-and-time adverbs ('more', 'less', 'longer', 'easily', 'fully', 'eventually', 'later', 'finally', 'quickly'). The syntactic frame and the described situation do not decide it: other verbs with nearly the same meaning stay at the pole's floor in an identical frame ('obtain', 'purchase', 'receive', 'deliver', 'repair', 'cook', 'eat', 'pay', 'teach', 'buy', 'win', 'lose', 'increase', 'reduce', 'know', 'learn', 'study', 'arrive', 'leave', 'stop' all measure 0.00-0.49), so label a token active iff it is in this lexical set (a lemma family counts as one entry), with the one positional modifier that these words fire ~6-14x more often when they sit in a predicate right after an auxiliary ('has/have/will/can/been') or an infinitival 'to'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
On the first Saturday of every month, the residents of Marlow Street close the road to traffic and set out folding tables along the curb. What started as a modest swap of seedlings and spare tools has grown into a neighborhood institution, with a lending shelf for board games, a repair bench for bicycles, and a small stage where children perform plays they rehearsed in garages.

The organizers hold no membership list. Anyone who shows up is handed a name tag and a task, and the tasks rotate so that the same people are not always stuck at the registration table. A retired carpenter named Ada Price supervises the repair bench. She inspects each bicycle, writes the fault on a chalkboard, and teaches whoever is curious how to adjust a brake cable. 'We are not a shop,' she says. 'We are a room full of neighbors who happen to own wrenches.'

The lending shelf started with forty games donated by a family whose children had outgrown them. Within a year it held nearly three hundred titles, catalogued on index cards in a wooden box. Borrowers sign the card, bring the box back on the following Saturday, and leave a note about which rules they ignored. Those notes are the closest thing the shelf has to a review section, and volunteers read them aloud during the last hour of the market.

Food is simple. A grill, a pot of beans, a tray of cornbread. The line forms early and moves fast because everyone knows the drill: collect a plate, greet the person behind you, and carry your dishes to the wash tub when you finish. Nobody is paid. The market covers its costs through a jar beside the grill and a yearly grant from the neighborhood association, which distributes the money in spring.

By midday the road smells of charcoal and cut grass. Teenagers drag folding chairs from the church basement, and older residents claim the shade beneath the maple. The event has become more popular each season, and the organizers have learned to plan for twice as many visitors as they expect. Last spring the association hired a coordinator for the first time. Her job is to help volunteers schedule their shifts, to protect the market from liability disputes, and to go after small grants that nobody else has time to pursue. She works from a desk at the back of the hardware store, surrounded by seed catalogues and a telephone that rings only on weekdays.

Winter is quieter. The grill is stored, the stage is dismantled, and the lending shelf moves into the church hall, where a single lamp stays lit above the index cards. In February the coordinator prints a one-page summary of the year: how many bicycles were repaired, how many games went home with new families, how much the jar collected. The numbers are modest, and she says so. What the page cannot record is the reason people keep showing up: the pleasure of a task done beside a neighbor, the small pride of a child who fixed a chain without assistance, the quiet that settles over the road when the tables are folded and the street belongs to traffic again.

explanation_scores.explanation: The positive pole is a retrospective lexical detector: it fires when the current token is one of a learned set of common English predicate words, above all everyday verb word-forms of the take/get/give/keep/help/make/find/save/protect/provide/create/turn/go/come/run/look/try/think family (and every inflection of them: take/takes/taking/took/taken, become/became/becomes, help/helps/helped, find/finds/found), plus a few degree-and-time adverbs ('more', 'less', 'longer', 'easily', 'fully', 'eventually', 'later', 'finally', 'quickly'). The syntactic frame and the described situation do not decide it: other verbs with nearly the same meaning stay at the pole's floor in an identical frame ('obtain', 'purchase', 'receive', 'deliver', 'repair', 'cook', 'eat', 'pay', 'teach', 'buy', 'win', 'lose', 'increase', 'reduce', 'know', 'learn', 'study', 'arrive', 'leave', 'stop' all measure 0.00-0.49), so label a token active iff it is in this lexical set (a lemma family counts as one entry), with the one positional modifier that these words fire ~6-14x more often when they sit in a predicate right after an auxiliary ('has/have/will/can/been') or an infinitival 'to'.
